criteria.title: Functional scope and what the ticks promise

levels.0: Lists 'send and receive messages' only, or spends time on stickers, calls and stories.
levels.1: Covers 1:1, groups, history, receipts and offline delivery, but never defines what one tick, two ticks and blue ticks guarantee.
levels.2: Covers 1:1, groups up to 500, multi-device history, presence and push, and defines the ticks precisely: one = durably stored, two = on a recipient device, blue = read, which later drives the persist-before-ack rule.

levels.0: No latency, ordering or durability targets.
levels.1: States the 500 ms delivery target and 'messages in order', without saying order within what, or what happens to gaps.
levels.2: Per-conversation total order identical on every device with detectable gaps, no loss after the first tick, under 500 ms p99 to online recipients, presence explicitly best-effort.

levels.0: No numbers, or numbers with no derivation.
levels.1: Gets about 230k messages/s but no peak, receipts or reconnect syncs.
levels.2: 500M × 40 ÷ 86,400 = 231k/s, 2× peak 463k/s; 1.9 recipients per message gives 880k deliveries/s at peak; receipts and syncs add up to about 1.16M requests/s at peak.

levels.0: Never estimates concurrent connections or storage.
levels.1: Estimates connections or storage, but sizes gateways by messages per second.
levels.2: 240M peak connections ÷ 500k per gateway = 480, 720 with a zone of headroom; 6 TB of messages a day, a 30-day hot tier of 540 TB replicated, and a cold tier for the rest.

levels.0: Only REST endpoints, with no persistent connection for delivery.
levels.1: A WebSocket with send and receive frames, but no client message ID, no acks, or no sync-on-reconnect call.
levels.2: WebSocket frames for send (with a client message ID), ack with sequence number, deliver, receipt cursors and presence; an HTTP sync endpoint with per-conversation cursors; media via presigned upload URLs.

levels.0: A single messages table with no partition key reasoning.
levels.1: Partitions messages by conversation, but uses a timestamp as the clustering key or ignores unbounded partitions.
levels.2: Messages keyed (conversation_id, bucket) with seq as the clustering key, per-user conversation rows holding last/delivered/read seq, a wide-column store chosen for write rate and per-partition range reads, plus hot/cold tiering.

criteria.title: Architecture and the send, deliver and sync paths

levels.0: Boxes with no walkthrough of a message.
levels.1: Walks a message from sender to an online recipient, but not offline delivery or reconnect sync.
levels.2: Walks send (gateway → conversation owner → persist → ack → fan-out log), delivery via the connection registry, offline push and reconnect sync, with a latency budget against 500 ms.

levels.0: Assumes the sender's server can send directly to any user.
levels.1: Mentions a user-to-gateway map, but not how it stays correct when connections move or gateways die.
levels.2: Connection registry with per-connection IDs and TTLs, gateways sized by memory and file descriptors, L4 balancing, and jittered reconnects so a gateway or zone loss does not become a reconnect storm.

levels.0: Orders by client or server timestamps.
levels.1: Uses a sequence number but does not say who assigns it or what happens when that owner fails.
levels.2: A single owner per conversation assigns gap-free seq numbers, persists before acking, re-derives the counter from the store on takeover, and breaks the rare double-owner tie deterministically by epoch.

levels.0: Delivers once and hopes; no offline plan.
levels.1: Stores messages for offline users and sends pushes, but per message, and duplicates are not handled.
levels.2: At-least-once delivery deduplicated by client message ID, receipts as monotonic cursors (max wins), sync by cursor on reconnect, and pushes collapsed per conversation to stay under the provider quota.

criteria.title: Group fan-out, presence and end-to-end encryption

levels.0: Broadcasts presence to all contacts and ignores encryption.
levels.1: Fans out group messages per member and notes E2EE exists, but without costs or consequences.
levels.2: Store once, fan out pointers (bounded by the 500-member cap), presence only to subscribed viewers with heartbeats at the gateway, and E2EE consequences: per-device keys, sender keys for groups, no server-side search or previews.

levels.1: Covers server and zone loss but not a reconnect storm, owner failover or push quota limits.
levels.2: Gives a zone-loss timeline with reconnect jitter and owner takeover, sizes the push quota, and at 10× names the fan-out log, inbox upserts and push quota first, plus multi-region home regions per conversation.

levels.1: Generic trade-offs (consistency vs availability) not tied to this design.
levels.2: Each decision (WebSocket vs polling, owner-assigned seq vs timestamps, persist-then-ack, store-once vs per-recipient copies, wide-column vs SQL, best-effort presence) comes with the alternative and why it lost here.
